Interviewer:	I’ll start by telling you a bit about what we’re doing. We’re basically looking at all women, in engineering, across the different disciplines and we’re mainly looking at people going on placement, but we are interviewing some people that aren’t going on placement as well. We’re looking at why women have chosen to go into the engineering industry and what they expect the industry to be like, and we’re going to compare that to what it is actually like when they are in the industry. We’re trying to improve women’s retention in the engineering industry (right). That’s basically the project that we’re working on but at the end of it all we’re hoping to put together a practical guidance document of recommendations that we can give to the engineering council and other engineering bodies as well.

Subject:	OK,

Interviewer:	So if it’s alright with you I’m going to ask you a bit about your background and why you wanted to do engineering, and things like that. So is it mechanical engineering that you’re doing?

Subject:	Yes, it is.

Interviewer:	Did you do A levels?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	What A levels did you do?

Subject:	Maths, Physics and English.

Interviewer:	OK, what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Er, a grammar school.

Interviewer:	OK, have you got any work experience in the industry already or any other work experience?

Subject:	Well, I’ve got work experience but not in engineering.

Interviewer:	OK. What do your parents do and are either of them engineers at all?

Subject:	Erm, my dad is a computer consultant, so he – he does a lot of – well he started off doing programming and that sort of thing then he worked his way up to management at the minute – background, computers is where he first started, he was the one who went on the degree course, ‘cos it sounded quite different.

Interviewer:	OK, why do you think that you’ve decided to study engineering then?

Subject:	Er, I felt that engineering would allow me to get out from behind a desk and perhaps try something a bit more practical, a bit (lost words) instead of – I mean it’s one of those things like you know, if the world ended and like there only a few people left and you have a lawyer, a businessman and an accountant and an engineer, who would be the most useful? It’d be an engineer, of course it would be and that’s always been sort of (?) do something – practically, make a difference in a way.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think there are any specific factors that influenced your decision, like your family, or the type of A levels that you did? Did you think about that kind of thing?

Subject:	I had an older brother, three years older than me, and he started university and did integrated engineering at [university] –so that I’ve got – my family is a – on my dad’s side – they’re all – because it’s seen as a (craft?) system and the craft is carpenters, which is kind of like engineers (yes) so they’re all into that sort of thing. My uncle built his own house and stuff and I’ve got cousins who are going into computers and stuff like that.

Interviewer:	OK, did you have any careers advice or anything like that when you were at school?

Subject:	Yes, go and be a town planner (laughter). How do they come up with these things? – I did really badly in my ‘A’ levels, I got an A in English, and an E in physics and an E in maths, because I didn’t really work very hard at them and I went to a Careers Advisor and she said, right, you’re interested in engineering are you? Yes, and I would actually like to go and do that, and she said well, why don’t you try looking at town planning instead? It’s very interesting you know and nah, no thank you.

Interviewer:	So they weren’t very supportive of the fact that you were interested in engineering?

Subject:	No, I mean like up to ‘A’ level, well the first year of ‘A’ level even, I wanted to be a lawyer. That’s why I had English in there, but it like when I, it’s quite (lost words) really. The only reason I picked Physics and Maths like that was ‘cos it – the subjects I wanted to do didn’t fit in with the timetable. I ended up like, oh, that’s alright then, I like doing those 2, I’ll do those. It was very random, perhaps not the ideal basis for studies.

Interviewer:	It is interesting how people end up in it – someone told me the other day that they ended up doing physics, because they had a bet with their mum, so you’re not the only one. You’ve said a bit about this already, but what do you think it is that really appeals to you about engineering?

Subject:	Well, it’s got the – it’s got the (?) – it’s got engineering in it and you sort of think, you think of things and you go out and see ‘em and you think that’s quite cool, it looks brilliant there, or how cool is that? Even when I used to get one of them pens and I’d think – you know when you used to get the propellor pencil, and my father came up with one and it was a push one, toward the end of the nib, you pushed and the nib came out. Who thought of that one? I’ve never seen that before. That’s a rather strange idea. Like the time when I was in American and came to this train station once and they had these seats, and er the back of the seat, when you leaned on the back of them, it had sort of a flexible back, so that actually it went backwards when you leaned back on it, but it supported you the same time, if you leaned back on it you wouldn’t fall over. The thing was wicked.

Interviewer:	So, it’s all fascinating to you really.

Subject:	Oh yes.

Interviewer:	What do you think it was that attracted you to mechanical engineering, rather than civil engineering or something like electrical engineering?

Subject:	I didn’t get the grades to do anything else. I did actually want to go on aero originally and then er – so I put my UCAS form in and went for aero and then I started reading more about what it involved and I went oh no, I really don’t want to do that. I thought, oh no. That was all I could think at the time (lost words) I really don’t want to do. Mechanical you can go into anything that you want to do. If you want to become a chemical engineer you can become a chemical engineer, or automotive or anything else.

Interviewer:	So it’s quite a broad base.

Subject:	Well you don’t know what it involves and you don’t know what it’s going to lead to. It’s quite hard for someone to specify what they’re going to do for the rest of their life in like one choice.

Interviewer:	OK, are you doing the sandwich course?

Subject:	Well I’m going on a year out – yeah.

Interviewer:	What – how did you decide to do that? (background noise)

Subject:	I spoke to a lot of people. I even went er – to one of those meetings, erm women in engineering. I met a girl there and she told me all about it and that was really good. And when I was in halls a lot of people, that I got put with in my block were a lot of finalists, and they’d all been on their year out and there was a lot of positive feedback that came back from it. And I thought, within myself that, I’m really not at all sure – well, I was kind of sure. I know what I really don’t like. I don’t know – well maybe if I did do that, in a job, it would be better. And maybe it was just having got it on with it as well, they’d learnt things so I thought I could do that (lost words).

Interviewer:	OK, how did you decide to come to [this] University?

Subject:	Well, I went to one of them – our schools (?) – a big hall, we had all the universities and they all had their own little stand and we had to walk round them and I didn’t see [this university] there at that. It was very strange. Er, but one day I was looking through UCAS book and I picked out everyone doing mechanical engineering. I think I looked more at the Times perhaps, the university thing in the Times, and [this university] was very high up. It was very good at sports and I thought to myself – and it was suitably far enough away from home, which is about 30 miles away. I didn’t want to be too close to home but I didn’t want to be too far away from home.

Interviewer:	That was the same with me (lost words) close enough to go home if you have to but far enough away so you’re not seeing your mum and dad every week.

Subject:	True, true. It as a nice university as well – when I first came here, it was so green, it was really nice. The buildings are nice and new it looked like – it looked like it knew what it was about.

Interviewer:	Yeah, Ok, when you decided to go into engineering, did you realise it was so male dominated?

Subject:	Yes, I think, I think I was a bit naïve – everyone kept telling me, are you’re sure you want to do that, you realise how many guys there are engineering and said like, I’m sure it won’t be that hard, you know. We’re in the 21st century now, it’s not gonna be a problem, we have equal rights, we have votes, I get on well with lads at school – what’s the difference? You learn. Oh dear, that was a big mistake, wasn’t it?

Interviewer:	Was it never a concern then really that there weren’t many women in engineering?

Subject:	You know – never that much, I think because of the way I was raised. If you want to do something, you do it, who cares if someone else is doing it as well? It’s all about your own progress and your own personal aspirations as to what you want to do. It’s only just the people round you – it’s nice if they’re nice too, and it would be pretty horrible if they were horrible and obviously, you know, that affects some things. I was kind of a bit self-absorbed at that age. (laughter)

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

Subject:	I don’t think that – either way – I mean, if someone wants to do engineering they should do engineering – if you’re interested in how things work and they feel like that’s the career that they’d like within themselves, then they should go and do it. I think there’s a lot of stereotypes as to what – I mean a lot of my friends didn’t even know what engineering was? They thought I was going to be a mechanic, in the past.

Interviewer:	Do you think there needs to be more information in the schools about what engineering is and that might help people make their minds up?

Subject:	I think – yeah. We were offered a 2 days thing – we stayed over at I think it was Imperial or something – a sort of women’s – I suppose for like women engineers, basically, we went along and it was like seminars and things, and I put my name down for that, but in the end I didn’t go to it. And there was that there. And all the girls in my – in a class of like 30 people – there were 4 girls – I’m like going ha, but we were all gonna go and gradually people went oh, I can’t go, I can’t go, I can’t go. And I didn’t really want to go by yourself anyway. Er, it probably – you really don’t know what it’s about who’ll do the course. You’ve just got no idea and don’t want to say oh engineering – you need to get maths for engineering, you really need to be able to do this. And you sort of say, yeah, and what? If you’re going to do it, you go ah, no. I thought I’d get away without learning that. I’ve got to learn it now.

Interviewer:	What characteristics then do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	It’s (?) isn’t it? I mean what makes a good employee you, should be asking. What separates engineers from other professional types. True, you have to know how things work, a thought to how things are designed and how to improve them.

Interviewer:	Do you think any of them things are particularly male traits or female traits or do you think it doesn’t matter?

Subject:	Well men are supposed to be better at, they’re better at special awareness and …

Interviewer:	Are they really or is that what people think?

Subject:	Well, psychological studies – that we’re supposed to be better at. It’s like men are physically stronger than women, it’s just one of them things. But we – I think – I’m a strong believer in you can do whatever you want to do. If you want to be better at something it just means you have to work a little bit harder than someone else. You have to train your mind to think that way. I mean obviously, English was my strongest suit ‘cos I got an A in it. And maths and physics – I couldn’t be bothered with it, they were a bit hard, so – but look at me, I’m in my 2nd year at uni, you don’t get there for nothing and plus I did a foundation year.

Interviewer:	Oh did you?

Subject:	Which helped me realise exactly- the essences of what I want to do. So you don’t just get to the 2nd year Mech Eng student just not being able to do Maths - it’s a matter of wanting to do something that badly, you’ve just got to apply yourself. It’s difficult – everyone’s different, that’s the trouble with that – if you’re looking for a general solution how to get women in engineering you’re gonna have to – I don’t know how you’d do it really.

Interviewer:	Do you think there are any advantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	I think – it feels quite bad really. You know, if I get stuck on something, a lot of lads who think – who feel like they have to come and help me, which is quite nice in respect, and they think oh y’know someone’s come to help me – the only reason why they’re helping me is because they’ve got this notion that, because I’m a girl, I can’t cope with things by myself.

Interviewer:	So how are they helping you? Quite patronising in a way really?

Subject:	In a way, but I’m grateful because I need the help. My brother has help – I’m not about to turn my head at help. I’ve not got that much pride that I’d turn down help, but and like if you’ve done something wrong it’s – perhaps if it’s a lad they’d get scorned for it, whereas if it’s a girl you kind of get ah, she’s only a girl. What’s she supposed to know about it? She’s not as good as everybody else. And that – that’s a bit harsh – you’re having to prove yourself continuously. When ever you go into a new group and more often than not – in fact every time - I’m surrounded by the fact – a group of (?) it’ll be 2 lads and me and they’ll not listen to your ideas and they’ll not take you seriously especially when you say things and you have to prove yourself every single time. I mean that has got better but the first year I was very very (?) experience of that, in this 2nd year I’ve got a really nice group and I think the lads are a bit more open-minded, a bit more mature – I’d rather (lost words).

Interviewer:	I was gonna ask you about the group work as well. Do you get into groups yourself or do you just get put into groups?

Subject:	Erm, 1st year we got put into groups, this year there’s a major project we’ve had – we’ve had – the lecturer picked out people that he’d deemed suitable as team leaders and then you had to sign yourself up against one of those names. I mean you all got put into groups so, we’re all a bit – it’s a industrial based project, and then each company – students were assigned to a company and then the company then gives you a problem to solve. So we’re all put in, we’re all split up and we’re all placed with a company and we’re given – that group of people, assigned to that company – certain people have been assigned as leaders for different groups, all working for the same company. And then we had to sign up our names against one of those leaders and one of the guys I worked with last year – that was my bad experience, I didn’t want to work with him again, the other lad my friend worked with last year. She said he was really good, so I was like I want to go with him. So I signed my name up (lost words)

Interviewer:	And the team leaders that were selected, were they generally men?

Subject:	I would say so, I think. I didn’t actually think of that at the time but yes. The trouble is that (?) if you’re the team leader you’re looking for some sort of erm knowledge about previous technical – like you might have worked on cars, you might know a bit about what’s going on in areas, all that kind of stuff. Girls don’t tend to – well I certainly – I still don’t – I’m learning now, but it’s only because I’m interested now, but I’ve no – they’ve got so much more confidence than us. I found that they were much more willing to go along and say that they knew something, even if they didn’t. It’d be like, you know, how do we do this? They’d say, oh I know how to do that and then come out with something and you’d think you know, and say, well I actually don’t know how to do this. I’m quite happy with someone else showing me how to do it. And they’re very confident in any ideas that they have, that they’re absolutely right and it’s always gonna work – and it’s not.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s just men in general or do you think that the women aren’t as confident because they are in a male environment?

Subject:	Personally, I would say I was about as confident of my ideas as they were but I couldn’t justify my confidence. I didn’t have the background knowledge to turn around and say to someone, this idea is definitely going to work because this equation shows this, this equation shows that. That was used in this previous product. I mean, I think girls are very much – they don’t make rash statements. They want to know that it’s right and it’s correct and you know, you can imagine (?) yourself when you come out of something, oh I’m right – I don’t have that problem.

Interviewer:	Ok, what was the bad experience of working in the group then? …

Subject:	 (I’d rather not say?). At the time it was working design project – for [company] – and we were put randomly into groups, a group of 5, me and my friend, both girls along with 3 of the lads. And we sat back on the design because we weren’t very confident and we didn’t really have any ideas, as a matter of fact (laughter) – it wasn’t what we were good at (yeah). It’s not that we’re girls and so we’re not good at it, it’s just that we’re not (?) – we prefer a different side of engineering to design. So when it came to an idea to move the sugar cube a certain distance along here, we had – we were coming up with ideas left, right and centre and we thought oh great, well this is nice that someone knows what they’re doing as well. But of course, they didn’t know what they were doing – they (lost words). So that went down first and then we got to the point where we had to virtually draw up our designs so we both went away and we said right, well cos’ you’ve done all the ideas, but we want to be part of the project as well, so we’ll go away and we’ll do these things on CAD so they gave us all the dimensions and we spent the whole weekend sitting on our – doing these autocad drawings and then when we met up the next week, they’d only gone away and changed the design and done the autocad drawings themselves and it was like, what? We’re all part of the designs really – because they had all the ideas and these 3 lads were friends, they used to go round each others houses a lot and they used to discuss things, like you do, and they’d come up with all these ideas and then make changes without consulting the rest of the group, which – I mean I’ve spoken to my dad about this and he was like – in this respect and he said, well they were only doing the project, which is true, they were but we weren’t included in that project.

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you think that’s because they were mates and knew each other? Do you think if there were 2 lads in the group and they were friends it would’ve been the same, or it would’ve been the women?

Subject:	I don’t know – I couldn’t say but I know that our ideas weren’t listened to when we did have ideas. That was one part, one part was moving the sugar cube about the circuit, the other part was (?) the sugar cube down. And [name] and I, she’s the other girl – came up with an idea. Oh great. Like a (lost words) candy sweets, and thought that’s a good idea. So we went out to a shop, found a (??) in a pound shop, brought it in and showed the lads it. Right, that would work a treat. I said right, let’s get on with this. And they said, yeah, yeah, we’ll just wait till – one lad wasn’t with us at the time – we’ll just wait till he comes back and then we can work on it. And we were working quick and I said we aren’t very happy – we’ve contributed to the project, a found an idea – it’s not a complete idea but what a good idea it is. It’s very simple and we could adapt that, sort of thing. Next week he’s gone away, he’s changed the design, he’s drawn it up and he comes in with his thing and that’s what we’re stuck with, ‘cos that’s his idea and that’s what he wants to do. It was a good idea, so we’re stuck with it – but whoa, you know we’re over here and we did something towards that but they just totally blanked us and took it as their own and didn’t include us in any of the design. Aah, they did my head in. The worst part – the reason – the fact that we ended up – we ended up in tears at the end of the project, we were so upset with how things had gone already, and the CAD drawings and we’d done so much work on it, and they’d just come up with something else and then the day before it had to be handed in we all got together to try and get this thing working. It had a lot of electrics in it – not electronic engineers, we didn’t really know what we were doing but (???) we tried to follow it and it wasn’t going too well and eventually we got something working but then one of the lads said, I want to go home. I really don’t want to stay here anymore. I can’t be bothered. We can do this tomorrow morning. And then [name] decided to get out. He put – he probably didn’t realise it was going to happen – he lifted the whole thing up and like everything fell apart and [name] and I were in the process of labelling the wires, so that we knew where to put them together the next time, but he just ripped it all – ruined all we’d done. We said well you can go home now as long as we come back early the next day because we had to show this guy – our lecturer – show him our model, the working model. We don’t (lost words) make our model work at 10 O’clock. So we had to meet early (??) so we can get everything working, and then we can be able to show it. They said, yeh yeh yeh we’re going home. We were like alright then, fine ok. Next day 9 O’clock they’re not there. Where are they? They’re not here, oh dear, now it’s got to 10 O’clock – they’re still not here and we have to show this whole thing at 10. So we said OK, we’ll go down to the lab, [name] and I, we were the only ones there and they still weren’t here. 10 past 10 – Oh look, you’ve finally turned up have you? Is it working? No, but we’ve managed to spray paint it and it looks very pretty. I’m like what the hell? So everyone else was showing off theirs, and we was fiddling with it and trying to get it right and eventually we were the last group and we had to show it and it wasn’t working, and [name] and I both went into tears, we were so frustrated we couldn’t do anything about it. They had the model, they had the (?). They did all the designs themselves, they went away and did the project by themselves, without including us and it didn’t matter how much we tried, how much we wanted to input into it, and offered our services and our help, they just didn’t care. They didn’t care enough, and they were always quite happy getting a C on their project, whereas [name] and I wanted an A - and that’s something about girls, you’ll find, that they’re much more likely to be high achievers because they want that. They want the A’s whereas the lads, oh it’s first year I don’t care – quite happy with a C, maybe even a D. Who would you (??) right. They think they’re right.

Interviewer:	Yes, do you think that they don’t realise that team work isn’t just about the final outcome but actually learning skills by working in a team? 

Subject:	No, I think they were more – they wanted results, they wanted to win their competition. They wanted theirs to be better to someone else’s. They were always comparing it with some other group. So we ended up crying in the department, going in the girls loos and one of the secretary’s spotted us, dragged us out. She was like, right, what’s going on? So we told her and she said right, I’m not having this in my department. What’s going on. Our lecturer gets dragged in and he’s very angry and he pulled the lads and in the end, and had a word with them and said, you know, don’t carry on like this in this department. They were just being lads – they were being immature lads about it. They were being – they were making their little groups, making their little pack and doing their own thing and that’s what lads do. And that’s something I’ve had to deal with and make sure it doesn’t happen again. But one of the lads, that was in that group, he was the worst lad out of all of them and he – pretty much the other 2 sorted – there’s always one, I think if he’s re-taking, I’m happy (laughter). I’m in the 2nd year, he’s back in the 1st year now because he did absolutely no work. I don’t think much about him at all.

Interviewer:	OK, so overall, the degree and the course, has it been what you’ve expected it to be?

Subject:	I’d say you don’t – I don’t think you can ever expect having to do this large amount of work. Whatever, I think doing engineering you sort of – you come out of A levels, you think God, that was much harder than GCSE’s, whereas God, A levels – hardest thing in the world. How can anything ever get harder than A levels? Then you go to degree level and you’re like aaargh, my goodness. How many subjects do I have to do? And how many tutorials and how many (??) and working in a group for the first time as well. Whenever I’ve worked in groups before – on school things, girls tend to stick together if you work in a group – well, it’s a load of girls, easy as that. You go do this, you go do that, I’d like to do this, is that OK? Yeah, Ok, fine, project done and thank you, A grade and there it is. Everyone wants to achieve high, and everyone wants to work together, and everyone can communicate fine and vice versa with the lads, the lads in my physics class worked together and they did it fine, and more often than not they’d get higher marks because they were brainy and intelligent, and we used to chat a lot (laugher). So it’s just – but I don’t think – I think both sexes aren’t used to working together. It must be worse for someone who’s come from an all boys school or an all girls school.

Interviewer:	Yes its interesting speaking to those people.

Subject:	But I don’t, I’ve been to a mixed school all my life, and being (?) doesn’t really matter does it. But then girls always stay with girls and boys always stay with boys.

Interviewer:	What do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far then?

Subject:	The course? The best things about the course – I really enjoy it and I get to do a large variety of subjects and I have some very, very intelligent lecturers, and amazing teachers amongst them. And I’ve met some amazing people through it, through coming to university and doing this degree and while I’ve been here I’ve met some amazing people, doing group work and all I think about these things and they come up with these ideas. (lost words)

Interviewer:	Yes, my next question’s probably related to that. Who or what do you think has been the biggest influence on you since you started this degree?

Subject:	I’d say the lecturers and er one lecturer – you always get one don’t you wherever – in my foundation year I had a lecturer called (name) and he was a hero actually. He was (??) actually and er this year well (??) the year before that – right, the first year was last year and I’ve had the same lecturer this year and he’s been to (?) university and he’s amazing too. But he’s a really good teacher and if you need to go and talk to him, he’s there for you.. I mean he’s had a chat to me, several times, you see and he says do you know what you’re doing here? ‘cos I’ll go to him, moaning about something and he’ll say, oh have you thought about it this way before and I’m like no, actually, I haven’t. (laughter) And I just need someone to just (lost words) and stop me focussing on myself and just sort of see the bigger picture, and know that it’s not all about you. The other students all seem to be having the same problem. And a lot of time when you blame someone else, it’s usually your own fault – not fault, but something you could have done yourself and I mean, that – going back to that first year project, I mean I blame the lads did a lot of that, but my fault as well. I was in that project, I was a part of that group. I could have done something perhaps or attempted to communicate a bit more, made it known to our lecturer beforehand that I wasn’t – that this was the situation, because it had been going on for some time and just try to talk and communicate more and try and become more involved in the design phase, and, at the time, I thought I was doing enough but the end result wasn’t likeable and maybe there was something else I could have done. I can’t say what,, no point really thinking about it, you can’t go back.

Interviewer:	Would you say that’s been the worst thing about the course? Is there anything else?

Subject:	I think – I think finding coming in to reality has been the worst thing on my course. Finding out that things aren’t as easy as you think they are and you might say to yourself, well if I’d have done that then I might have got those marks, but then when you go to try to do it, it’s really quite hard and that’s why no-one usually does do it, you know, it takes a lot of time and effort. It – the people I think – the lads that I was working with, in the first year, were fairly nice lads. When I spoke to them out of uni or whatever, it was nice chat and I wouldn’t have thought anything bad about them. It was just when you worked with them, they had this strange attitude but I think they would have got out of that by now. I think people do grow – I think I’ve probably grown up. I probably came in here, really quite naïve and now I’m a bit more wise, hopefully.

Interviewer:	Are you pleased that you chose this course then?

Subject:	Very much so. What really made me say that was, since I (?) my eyes out wanting to be a lawyer oh, since I was 13 years old. Right, I’m gonna go do law and earn lots of money and go to court and all this sort of thing. And they have like this thing at uni – at school – where they have this like mock court and actually (lost words) oh I was shocking. I forgot what I was doing and I was really nervous and it was absolutely awful and then I started to re-think things after that, was that what I really wanted to do? But you know, well I could be wrong and then I changed it here and changed it there and I had a law module this year and it is the most boring thing in the world, and there’s no right or wrong answer either and you know, and my goodness - our lecturer gave this citation about this guy who’d hit a golf ball and it’d bounced off a tree and hit another guy on the head. And the guy who got hit on the head sued the golfer. The guy that got hit on the head won, because the golfer who’d hit the ball, which had accidentally hit the tree, and hit the guy on the head, should have realised that that was possible - that he might have hit someone. How can you aim at a tree?

Interviewer:	You wouldn’t play golf at all, would you?

Subject:	 (lost words) I thought oh my goodness, that’s ridiculous and just listening to his lecture, go on about it and all these silly little niggles and things, and technicalities and with engineering you know…?

Interviewer:	You know where you are.

Subject:	Yeah. This table’s gonna go if the stress is too much. You know, if that’s gonna blow up should I change the flow rate? You know – right and wrong, right and wrong. And I thought perhaps – I know it’s not always black and white and there’s a lot of chopping and changing and making it as best as you can but at least you know that’s meant to be. Power – ah, it did my head in that lecture.

Interviewer:	It sounds bizarre. Have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Subject:	Oh dear, yes. I was taught by [name] unfortunately. It’s very depressing – in fact, she’s the only female lecturer I’ve ever had and she made such a poor show of herself, but had a lot of extenuating circumstances. She was pregnant at the time and she was probably having emotional problems or something – she was a bit weird and she went off on one every 2 minutes and then was normal again. So it was (?) the fact that (sighs)

Interviewer:	Would you have liked to have more female lecturers then? Would you have found that encouraging to have female lecturers?

Subject:	If I had a female lecturer who knew her subject as well as my other lecturers do – and if I ask them a question, they can answer it just like that and I knew that they knew what they were talking about I wouldn’t mind. I don’t care who I get taught by. I don’t find it – I find every lecturer that I’ve ever spoken to, thoroughly helpful and very able to help me and willing to help me and that’s why they’re lecturers. And a lot of lecturers are like that. The reason why they go into academia is to teach and be happy with it. Some lecturers concentrate more on the research side but I don’t think it matters if it’s a woman or man, so…

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of the lecturers treat you differently because you’re female?

Subject:	Yes, quite frequently and I quite like it (laughter). Did you ever wonder what happens when the lads are coming to a door and they’re both about to go through the same door – did you ever wonder? If you’re a girl and there’s a lad there, they open the door, so you walk through, have you ever wondered what lads do? But er, I’ve got – yeah – one lecturer, he did treat us – not, not inferior but he does give us a lot more leeway than he’d give the lads. He’d expect the lads to know things like that whereas with the girls he’s sort of like oh you don’t know it? Oh, OK. I think there’s a lot of fear on the lecturers part – I think there’s a lot of fear there, because a somebody could turn round and accuse them of sexism and of picking on girls and all this kind of stuff, so they just tend to leave us alone. 

Interviewer:	So they’re not really used to having females in their environment, do you think?

Subject:	I don’t think they – it’s not like they mind it, not so much used to them – one student’s much the same as anyone else. It’s a political thing that comes up time and time again. You hear these silly stories abut people getting sued for sexual harassment and this and that, and you know, it’s quite frightening what some malicious individuals would do to some poor guy who was only trying to help, a lot of the time. Speaking like (lost words) I think they have to be quite cautious about how they have to go about things as well, purely because of the legal situation and that kind of thing. 

Interviewer:	OK, do you think there’s any particular aspects of the university teaching or the advice that you’ve had that’ll help you when you go on placement?

Subject:	I think its going to be absolutely different

Interviewer:	In what way?

Subject:	In that, if I had a rubbish group member, they’d get fired. Don’t have to put up with them being slack and stupid all the time. I’ve got one at the moment, I’m a bit bitter. But, you know they’re professional – that’s what it’s about. It’s about being a professional, lecturer style, I mean – you’re not gonna learn like that when you’re in one of the companies, you’re gonna learn from experience as opposed to tutorial questions.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think that any skills that you’ve learnt on the course will help you?

Subject:	Skills? Skills like report writing, yeah? That should help. Then there’s a certain degree of having to sit down and do work, and that will probably come in useful. Communication skills, of course, from work. So yeah. (laughter)

Interviewer:	Er, have the university done much to help prepare you for the placement, do you think?

Subject:	Ah, I’ve got a cracking Careers Advisor, [placement coordinator], she’s fantastic. Every 2 minutes she’s got emails coming out to you about the jobs and such like. She’s always telling me about email sites and the career service is really quite good. They’ve got a list of all these sites you can go to which helps you like – Doctor Job and that kind of thing. So they give you advice on those and like, lots of web links and information – so I feel totally prepared like – well the interview process and the CV process, perhaps not the job but I don’t think you could really be prepared for the job because it’d be so different every time. Working environment – it’s going to be different anyway, and that again depends on the company and the culture that’s within that company.

Interviewer:	OK, do you know where you’re going on placement yet?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Have you applied to lots of different companies?

Subject:	I have, but my grades are pants so no-one really wants me. I’ve applied to loads of them – still applying. I had an interview and got rejected from that and I’ve got another one on 31st March for the company that I’m doing the project with at the moment.
Interviewer:	OK, yeah.

Subject:	But I really want to go and work for an oil company but oh…

Interviewer:	And why did you want to go and work for an oil company?

Subject:	Partly to get my big (?) line and flow rate and you get your filters and your pump and it’s like wow – yeah, that’d be cool. Anything like process engineering, for a chemical company – that’ll do just as well.

Interviewer:	What do you think that you’ll get out of going on placement?

Subject:	Erm, something to put on my CV. Experience working and doing a project. Wherever I do work, I mean like, if you went to a company and you had to work on the computer all day. You’d probably be really good at like the computers and things like that. So whatever you’re going to be doing you’ll be really good at and, you can contribute towards your course. It ‘s a year towards your Chartership if you go with (?) of your sponsored ones. You get the possibility of getting a job afterwards. And a year out where you can think about thing and just like, I don’t have to go home and do tutorials, you can just sit back and watch telly or get a video, icecream and some pizza, a bottle of wine – yeah.

Interviewer:	So have you had any particular criteria where you’ve been looking at the companies to apply to – like the pay or you know, you said about (?)

Subject:	My situations a bit different. Because of my A level grades are so rubbish they give me a total number of points of 14 UCAS points, which is really quite pants when everyone else is asking for 18, (really?) just to get through an application form. And I even when I don’t give the minimum number of UCAS points, what are they going to do when they pick up the form? Oh look, someone who’s got 3 A’s at such and such – really important subjects towards our degree, and somebody’s got that. I mean here, the average last year was about 56. It’s not a lot, it’s just average. So rubbish ‘A’ level grades, average year, average …

Interviewer:	Do you think that the Foundation year has made up at all for the A levels?

Subject:	On a personal note, it meant a lot to me, that – I was very worried – I mean after ‘A’ levels my confidence just went whack! There was no confidence, I didn’t think I’d get anything. And my Foundation year I wanted to do – to really prove to myself that the fact I could do something, if I worked at it. And I did do that I got 75% in Maths and I got 76% in physics and materials so I felt a little bit better and I actually did the work for a change. And that was important to me. If I’d failed those then I would have known that I was a really silly (wench?) and it’s true that maths and physics are a really big part of engineering, and if you can’t do them, then there’s really no point in doing engineering because you’d struggle and probably like you’d not be happy with it either. It’s probably just not suited to you at all, but I know I can do it and that’s what that foundation year meant to me. But a lot of companies don’t take it into account. You have like this special section that say special considerations, any other information you’d like to give, and that’s where my foundation year goes, you know, underneath my A level results. I could imagine someone having 50 pages of form and going Oh my God no, Oh my God no, we won’t have her. There’s no point in looking back on it and going if, if if if if if, you’ve got to go with it. You’ve got to do your CV and your covering letter instead of the application forms and you’ve got to pick out companies and ring them up and say right this is my situation would you give me a chance, would you have a chat to me at least, get me an interview and then decide whether to shove me out. I mean fair enough after an interview, you’ve got a better view of my personal personality. I do a lot of extra curricular activities – I’ve done a lot of stuff. I’ve been to Camp America, so y’know.

Interviewer:	I think you’ve actually answered some of these questions – what do you think will be the best and the worst things about going on placement?

Subject:	Erm, best things – experience, meeting more people, possibility of getting a job afterwards, a year working towards accreditation and your Chartered Engineer status. Hopefully moving closer to my boyfriend and taking time out from school work – well Uni work. Worst things – moving away, being amongst old people, older people – sorry if you’re listening, you know what I mean. You’re used to being around 20/25 year olds and then suddenly you’re with 40 year old. Having to live away from everyone you know and just set up house, on my own, really not knowing anyone at all and finding things that you really want to do, like for me it’d be like finding a karate club somewhere because if I didn’t have one I’d be really quite depressed. I want to enjoy myself – which I mean to do. Just sit on my butt all day doing things – worried about making friends and that kind of things.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you think that work is going to differ from university in terms of what is expected of you and how you are treated?

Subject:	Er, depends on which company you work for. Well I think – I can imagine going to a company and getting treated much – with much more respect than I would do at university. And having a lot more responsibility and being considered as an equal, on a par with someone else. But I can imagine it going the other way as well that they’ve got a set programme for a student and that they consider you like oh, they’ve not got a degree yet, we’re gonna be easy on them, and just get treated as like doing the degree. In some respects I can see how it would be (yeah) get a lot more respect.

Interviewer:	So it might just depend on the company you’re with?

Subject:	Definitely and I’m prepared for that. (lost words)

Interviewer:	In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

Subject:	A lot more knowledge, a lot more business sense, a lot more character. Er, hopefully a Chartered Engineer. I will be much more confident in what I do, I think, because a lot of the time you do you’re uni work, and you get it wrong a lot of the time, because you’re just learning it for the first time. You go into industry – 5 years time, it’ll be like, I’ve done that before, I got it right.

Interviewer:	Where do you see yourself in 10 years time? Do you think you’ll still be in the engineering industry?

Subject:	You never can tell. From what I’ve heard once you get your chartered engineer, it depends what you do as well because I mean you could go into management, a lot of engineers do.

Interviewer:	Are you interested in that?

Subject:	Not particularly but you’ll end up there one way or another. You work hard, you go into management, that’s what happens.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s what should happen?

Subject:	No, I think you should get a decent amount of pay packet for the skills that you have. Well that would happen if – if you became – if you weren’t stuck with the company and you became like a contractor – only if you wanted that kind of lifestyle, I don’t think I would. Purely cos my Dad does it and I’ve seen what it does to him, he goes round to companies and he can command huge amounts of pay just for doing a very – a rush job. I think it’s ‘cos you know you are in demand and if someone else is a bit busy, and I don’t know what. But it would be quite nice to travel round a bit I think – definitely. Ten years time – mortgage, kids. That’s the trouble, what do you do with your kids?

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think that’s a problem with having a career?

Subject:	Oh yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s particularly for the industry you’ve chosen or do you think it’d be the same for any other industry?

Subject:	I don’t think it would matter if you were an accountant, a lawyer or what. I think being a woman, having kids. Perhaps some women don’t feel like they want to look after their kids but for me personally, I’d want to be there for them. I’d want to look after them and I don’t think I could do that kind of good job with them and go 9 to 5 in an office. I’d need some sort of flexi time and some sort of home working scheme, so I don’t know whether that’d be possible in the engineering industry. It’s like you have on-going projects and a lot of the time, you probably need to be on site, if it were a plant, or if it were something – the development of some sort of product – you’d need to be clued up with what’s going on and again you’d need to be sure and for me (lost words).

Interviewer:	Do you think there is anything in the way that engineering is set up that could be changed so that it is more flexible?

Subject:	I don’t have enough experience of working in the industry to say that really. I’ve no experience of, and I’m sure different companies work differently once you get into them, it depends on the company. I don’t know. To make women stay you’d have to, if she wanted to (?) and have a family you’d have to make that easier for her and give her sometime with the kids. I mean if she wanted to go and pick her kids up from school, give her an hour off to pick her kids up from school. It wouldn’t take that long, unless you work in in London. And just the little things like that and maybe only working 3 days a week instead of 5, and you know, just working shorter days maybe, so that she could go and pick her kids up and then take them straight home and make dinner for them and whatever. Then you could just work – work like a schoolteacher does really. That’d be ideal, that’s why a lot of women do go into teaching isn’t it? Cos you know kids are in school, you’re in school and that’s fine - that’d be quite nice I would imagine.

Interviewer:	Ok, what sort of job would be your ideal job?

Subject:	A very cool job, lets start dreaming! My job – my ideal job would be if I could – I think I would like to travel but not for years, kind of like a month would be OK – 2 weeks would be quite nice just to go away and do a bit of a project and have a bit of holiday time there as well just for the weekend or something, going (?) and back and er, have my little cosy house and my (?) and er if I had a job that had prospects so I could kind of make myself useful in the company and could have a good pay structure so I could increase my earnings, when I deserved it – it’d be interesting, it’d have different types of projects and perhaps I could move round departments well. Just a flexible job is all I need – that’s all I want.

Interviewer:	That’s – are you likely to achieve that?

Subject:	No, ‘cos that’s to dream – that’s like the ideal (?) – that’s never gonna happen.

Interviewer:	Why not?

Subject:	Why not? Because I – oh, I keep forgetting words – like you’ve got to er weigh things up and you can have something nice in one area, but you’ve got to sacrifice something in another area. ‘Cos there’s no way that – I mean, I first of all, if you want to travel a lot, or just for 2 years, if had kids, you’d have to leave them for 2 years – that’s not much is it? If you wanted to move round departments, but then suddenly got interested in one department, you’d be like oh no, I’ve got this department, I’m quite happy where I am. So you can’t sort of say, I want a job which lets me move round departments, then you find something you like, no, I don’t want to do that now, and then now, I do, then now, I don’t because you can see that’d get very confusing and the employer wouldn’t know whether they were coming or going. Purely, because of human nature I think, because as soon as you’ve got something, you think oh, I wonder if I could get better, you know.

Interviewer:	The grass is always greener?

Subject:	Yeah, and it mightn’t be – you might lose out and be unhappy. Or you might like to stay where you are forever, and then the people around you might not want you to stay there, for whatever reason. And it’s difficult for me to think, well it’s difficult with er our lecturer (name) when she’d gone on maternity leave. She had 2 kids very close together, it completely screwed up our lectures and she hadn’t marked some work or something and exams came out (later?) and all this kind of stuff and she was personal tutor for a project, which is over 2 terms, so she’s only here for the 1st term, and now she’s on maternity leave with her baby so she’s not there for the 2nd term. And that’s the same kind of thing you’d find in industry, she started a project and now she can’t finish it, now they’ve got to find someone else. Why would you employ someone who you know, is gonna be off doing that and messing up your company and making things way more difficult than they have to be, just because they’re a woman? Because that’s what they do. I mean you wouldn’t would you? It’s a bit like why would they want to employ me if they had someone with better ‘A’ level grades.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that generally the career prospects are good in your field of engineering?

Subject:	Phew, I’m a bit confused. I’ve had people telling me there’s a recession on and people telling me there’s a lack of engineers, especially women engineers and I’d be better off because I’m a woman engineer – I’m just a bit confused as to which one it is. Is there a recession? Or am I in quite a good position? I’m really not quite sure at the moment.

Interviewer:	Fair enough. Are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far?

Subject:	I think yeah – I would have perhaps – somewhere with hindsight, I don’t really know what happened. I thought about a couple of things – I couldn’t be sure if I would actually do it right, like my ‘A’ levels, if I’d done more arty subjects, and then those are my stronger subjects but perhaps I would have got better ‘A’ level grades and then I could have done the foundation year, like I did anyway, you know, in engineering. But, at the same time the foundation year wouldn’t have been as easy because I did A level maths and physics, but I would have had the ‘A’ level grades you see and then now I could go to a company and say look at my ‘A’ level grades, aren’t they amazing?

Interviewer:	And then that seems total madness as well then saying well, they’re only interested in your grades and it doesn’t matter what the subject is at ‘A’ level.

Subject:	I think when you’ve got that many people applying to you, you’re allowed to make that sort of choice.

Interviewer:	What if…

Subject:	Well there are many what ifs but I don’t think you can think like that with regards to the future. Hmm, what if I do this in the future? You can say to yourself, hmm, if I’d done that…

Interviewer:	What 5 words would you use to describe the culture or the characteristics of the engineering industry?

Subject:	The industry? Like as whole (yeah) – the whole, entire industry? Oh well, technical, er 

Interviewer:	It doesn’t matter if you can’t find 5 exactly.

Subject:	OK, (?) and technical. What kind of words are you looking for?

Interviewer:	Descriptive words?

Subject:	Adjectives?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	The industry. Well, its doing quite badly at the moment so bad (laughter) I think it’s going – progressive – like it’s always changing, you know (yeah), always moving forward, you hope so, anyway. I think that’ll do.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it is masculine?

Subject:	I think – I think it depends how you define it really, like if you’re talking about is the industry dominated by males then yes. If you’re talking about is it possible for women to do the job, then I’d say it’s very possible for women to do the job. (Yeah) If you’re saying that the subject is masculine, like engineering as a whole is masculine and you think like that, because you’re a male. I disagree, I’d say you can think any way you want to think.

Interviewer:	Do you think people …

Subject:	Perceive it like that? (yeah). I’d say so, yeah.

Interviewer:	Yeah, and do you think that’s mainly people who don’t really know what the industry is or people in the industry as well?

Subject:	I think – I think it’s natural. If you see loads of men around you then you’re gonna assume that a man’s gonna come to the job and that’s – there’s the idea of that – I mean, it feels (really male?), and my mother’s generation were told to be nurses, or what have you and it’s changed now and it’s only now that it’s changed, so it’s going to take a while for that to filter through. I mean, just like any other industry, women have been incorporated very successfully I’m sure.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the situation will get better then?

Subject:	I don’t know. I think – I think there is some very girly girls out there, who perhaps really don’t want to be involved in something – well, it does involve getting your hands dirty and it does involve fiddling around with things and asking how things work. (lost words)

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you think that there is a certain type of girl that chooses to do engineering?

Subject:	Probably. I would say I’m a Tom-girl. I mean you’ve just got to walk into the library to notice the difference. You see all the mech engines and engineering students walking around in scruffy clothes and big jumpers, just ‘cos you’re rushing around all day and you don’t have time to put your make up on and do your hair. Who really cares anyway, you know? And the you go up a level to the psychology level and you think Oh my God, I’ve done my hair nicely, I’ve got my make up on, got my posh shoes – got no time to go shopping me but they do. They get all these nice belts and earrings and (?) but you know? (laughter)

Interviewer:	Do you think that women in the industry think that they can’t be feminine?

Subject:	I’d say not. I think it’s a very valuable tool. I would say you can get a lot out of being a woman and you can (lost words). I mean Maggie Thatcher and politics – prime example. Fantastic, you know, and I mean she was mad, but – you know, (lost words) she went around wearing skirts and brooches and all sorts – do their hair nicely (laughter). (Yeah) Well fine until her A’s – not something I would probably do myself. ‘Cos no, she was a hard nailed woman and she knew how to play men, she really knew how to use her femininity to her advantage and that’s what being a woman’s all about.

Interviewer:	Do you think any aspect of the engineering culture will be problematic for you?

Subject:	I think if I find people who are ignorant and not as (wealthy?) as they would like to feel that they are, there could be a problem. I think that – I’m not so naïve as to say that all the problems are (?) that there isn’t any sexism within the industry anymore, but I’d say its a lot better than it was (yeah) and anyone from my generation would know sort of like that that’s not permittable. You know, that’s not – that’s not good anymore but to be fair you get 50 year olds and 60 year old manager, perhaps they’re not so used to it. They might find it a bit of a problem – it depends on people, doesn’t it? Some people, you still find people that support the Nazis, and y’know it’s a freaky world, so you just never know what you’re gonna come up against. As long as you handle it, y’know, in the correct manner, and in a sensible manner as well.

Interviewer:	How do you think that you will deal with it if anything like that happens to you?

Subject:	If I felt I was being neglected perhaps or not given the kind of work that I’d like, that’s something I’d make sure of when I started work – I’d make sure that they have got the systems in place to deal with things like that. A lot of companies do take it seriously now. It would take a lot of strength for a woman to go away and say I want this investigated. But I think – I think to be a woman in engineering nowadays, you have to have a lot of character, and you have to have a lot of confidence in yourself and that you were right and that you could have those problems sorted out. And if you do have that – you have to be confident purely to inspire confidence and until you show that you’re not as confident as them, they’ll take advantage of you and they’ll just be…you’ve just got to be as big and loud as you can be. In fact, or the other way be quiet and demure and come in with a quip, every now and then and maybe then they’ll be like, ah she’s quite (one?) to watch out for. Y’know, one of them.

Interviewer:	OK, the last thing that I’ve got to ask you is do you think that as an engineering student your educational experience differs from other students (yes) who are studying Social Science or Geography?

Subject:	Yes (laughter) Big time, loads of hours, I have like a silly amount of hours, I think I’m up to 30 hours one week and it’s like madness.

Interviewer:	Is that a good thing or a bad thing that you have more hours?

Subject:	It pushes you. It pushes you so much and that’s fine because (Lost words)

Interviewer:	Do you think it makes it easier when you actually go into work, if you have had as much structured time?

Subject:	I’ve heard from people that are graduating right now, that at university, especially with engineering is too technical, we have to cram so much into such a short bit of time but er you’re (?) and you’re working really hard and everyone in a company is really impressed with you because you can do the work as quickly. It’s only because they’ve got lazy and they don’t feel like doing it anymore and they slow down but you’re still working at this pace, that you do at university and eventually you calm it down and work at their pace ‘cos its easier and its accepted, so why not? I’ve heard that from a couple of people.

Interviewer:	Well thank you very much.

turns.text: OK, why do you think that you’ve decided to study engineering then?
