turns.text: Er, I felt that engineering would allow me to get out from behind a desk and perhaps try something a bit more practical, a bit (lost words) instead of – I mean it’s one of those things like you know, if the world ended and like there only a few people left and you have a lawyer, a businessman and an accountant and an engineer, who would be the most useful? It’d be an engineer, of course it would be and that’s always been sort of (?) do something – practically, make a difference in a way.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think there are any specific factors that influenced your decision, like your family, or the type of A levels that you did? Did you think about that kind of thing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I had an older brother, three years older than me, and he started university and did integrated engineering at [university] –so that I’ve got – my family is a – on my dad’s side – they’re all – because it’s seen as a (craft?) system and the craft is carpenters, which is kind of like engineers (yes) so they’re all into that sort of thing. My uncle built his own house and stuff and I’ve got cousins who are going into computers and stuff like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you have any careers advice or anything like that when you were at school?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, go and be a town planner (laughter). How do they come up with these things? – I did really badly in my ‘A’ levels, I got an A in English, and an E in physics and an E in maths, because I didn’t really work very hard at them and I went to a Careers Advisor and she said, right, you’re interested in engineering are you? Yes, and I would actually like to go and do that, and she said well, why don’t you try looking at town planning instead? It’s very interesting you know and nah, no thank you.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So they weren’t very supportive of the fact that you were interested in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I mean like up to ‘A’ level, well the first year of ‘A’ level even, I wanted to be a lawyer. That’s why I had English in there, but it like when I, it’s quite (lost words) really. The only reason I picked Physics and Maths like that was ‘cos it – the subjects I wanted to do didn’t fit in with the timetable. I ended up like, oh, that’s alright then, I like doing those 2, I’ll do those. It was very random, perhaps not the ideal basis for studies.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It is interesting how people end up in it – someone told me the other day that they ended up doing physics, because they had a bet with their mum, so you’re not the only one. You’ve said a bit about this already, but what do you think it is that really appeals to you about engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, it’s got the – it’s got the (?) – it’s got engineering in it and you sort of think, you think of things and you go out and see ‘em and you think that’s quite cool, it looks brilliant there, or how cool is that? Even when I used to get one of them pens and I’d think – you know when you used to get the propellor pencil, and my father came up with one and it was a push one, toward the end of the nib, you pushed and the nib came out. Who thought of that one? I’ve never seen that before. That’s a rather strange idea. Like the time when I was in American and came to this train station once and they had these seats, and er the back of the seat, when you leaned on the back of them, it had sort of a flexible back, so that actually it went backwards when you leaned back on it, but it supported you the same time, if you leaned back on it you wouldn’t fall over. The thing was wicked.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, it’s all fascinating to you really.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think it was that attracted you to mechanical engineering, rather than civil engineering or something like electrical engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I didn’t get the grades to do anything else. I did actually want to go on aero originally and then er – so I put my UCAS form in and went for aero and then I started reading more about what it involved and I went oh no, I really don’t want to do that. I thought, oh no. That was all I could think at the time (lost words) I really don’t want to do. Mechanical you can go into anything that you want to do. If you want to become a chemical engineer you can become a chemical engineer, or automotive or anything else.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So it’s quite a broad base.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well you don’t know what it involves and you don’t know what it’s going to lead to. It’s quite hard for someone to specify what they’re going to do for the rest of their life in like one choice.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you doing the sandwich course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well I’m going on a year out – yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What – how did you decide to do that? (background noise)

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I spoke to a lot of people. I even went er – to one of those meetings, erm women in engineering. I met a girl there and she told me all about it and that was really good. And when I was in halls a lot of people, that I got put with in my block were a lot of finalists, and they’d all been on their year out and there was a lot of positive feedback that came back from it. And I thought, within myself that, I’m really not at all sure – well, I was kind of sure. I know what I really don’t like. I don’t know – well maybe if I did do that, in a job, it would be better. And maybe it was just having got it on with it as well, they’d learnt things so I thought I could do that (lost words).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how did you decide to come to [this] University?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, I went to one of them – our schools (?) – a big hall, we had all the universities and they all had their own little stand and we had to walk round them and I didn’t see [this university] there at that. It was very strange. Er, but one day I was looking through UCAS book and I picked out everyone doing mechanical engineering. I think I looked more at the Times perhaps, the university thing in the Times, and [this university] was very high up. It was very good at sports and I thought to myself – and it was suitably far enough away from home, which is about 30 miles away. I didn’t want to be too close to home but I didn’t want to be too far away from home.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That was the same with me (lost words) close enough to go home if you have to but far enough away so you’re not seeing your mum and dad every week.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: True, true. It as a nice university as well – when I first came here, it was so green, it was really nice. The buildings are nice and new it looked like – it looked like it knew what it was about.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, Ok, when you decided to go into engineering, did you realise it was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I think, I think I was a bit naïve – everyone kept telling me, are you’re sure you want to do that, you realise how many guys there are engineering and said like, I’m sure it won’t be that hard, you know. We’re in the 21st century now, it’s not gonna be a problem, we have equal rights, we have votes, I get on well with lads at school – what’s the difference? You learn. Oh dear, that was a big mistake, wasn’t it?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was it never a concern then really that there weren’t many women in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: You know – never that much, I think because of the way I was raised. If you want to do something, you do it, who cares if someone else is doing it as well? It’s all about your own progress and your own personal aspirations as to what you want to do. It’s only just the people round you – it’s nice if they’re nice too, and it would be pretty horrible if they were horrible and obviously, you know, that affects some things. I was kind of a bit self-absorbed at that age. (laughter)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think that – either way – I mean, if someone wants to do engineering they should do engineering – if you’re interested in how things work and they feel like that’s the career that they’d like within themselves, then they should go and do it. I think there’s a lot of stereotypes as to what – I mean a lot of my friends didn’t even know what engineering was? They thought I was going to be a mechanic, in the past.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there needs to be more information in the schools about what engineering is and that might help people make their minds up?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think – yeah. We were offered a 2 days thing – we stayed over at I think it was Imperial or something – a sort of women’s – I suppose for like women engineers, basically, we went along and it was like seminars and things, and I put my name down for that, but in the end I didn’t go to it. And there was that there. And all the girls in my – in a class of like 30 people – there were 4 girls – I’m like going ha, but we were all gonna go and gradually people went oh, I can’t go, I can’t go, I can’t go. And I didn’t really want to go by yourself anyway. Er, it probably – you really don’t know what it’s about who’ll do the course. You’ve just got no idea and don’t want to say oh engineering – you need to get maths for engineering, you really need to be able to do this. And you sort of say, yeah, and what? If you’re going to do it, you go ah, no. I thought I’d get away without learning that. I’ve got to learn it now.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What characteristics then do you think make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s (?) isn’t it? I mean what makes a good employee you, should be asking. What separates engineers from other professional types. True, you have to know how things work, a thought to how things are designed and how to improve them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think any of them things are particularly male traits or female traits or do you think it doesn’t matter?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well men are supposed to be better at, they’re better at special awareness and …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they really or is that what people think?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, psychological studies – that we’re supposed to be better at. It’s like men are physically stronger than women, it’s just one of them things. But we – I think – I’m a strong believer in you can do whatever you want to do. If you want to be better at something it just means you have to work a little bit harder than someone else. You have to train your mind to think that way. I mean obviously, English was my strongest suit ‘cos I got an A in it. And maths and physics – I couldn’t be bothered with it, they were a bit hard, so – but look at me, I’m in my 2nd year at uni, you don’t get there for nothing and plus I did a foundation year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oh did you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Which helped me realise exactly- the essences of what I want to do. So you don’t just get to the 2nd year Mech Eng student just not being able to do Maths - it’s a matter of wanting to do something that badly, you’ve just got to apply yourself. It’s difficult – everyone’s different, that’s the trouble with that – if you’re looking for a general solution how to get women in engineering you’re gonna have to – I don’t know how you’d do it really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there are any advantages to being a woman engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think – it feels quite bad really. You know, if I get stuck on something, a lot of lads who think – who feel like they have to come and help me, which is quite nice in respect, and they think oh y’know someone’s come to help me – the only reason why they’re helping me is because they’ve got this notion that, because I’m a girl, I can’t cope with things by myself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So how are they helping you? Quite patronising in a way really?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In a way, but I’m grateful because I need the help. My brother has help – I’m not about to turn my head at help. I’ve not got that much pride that I’d turn down help, but and like if you’ve done something wrong it’s – perhaps if it’s a lad they’d get scorned for it, whereas if it’s a girl you kind of get ah, she’s only a girl. What’s she supposed to know about it? She’s not as good as everybody else. And that – that’s a bit harsh – you’re having to prove yourself continuously. When ever you go into a new group and more often than not – in fact every time - I’m surrounded by the fact – a group of (?) it’ll be 2 lads and me and they’ll not listen to your ideas and they’ll not take you seriously especially when you say things and you have to prove yourself every single time. I mean that has got better but the first year I was very very (?) experience of that, in this 2nd year I’ve got a really nice group and I think the lads are a bit more open-minded, a bit more mature – I’d rather (lost words).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I was gonna ask you about the group work as well. Do you get into groups yourself or do you just get put into groups?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, 1st year we got put into groups, this year there’s a major project we’ve had – we’ve had – the lecturer picked out people that he’d deemed suitable as team leaders and then you had to sign yourself up against one of those names. I mean you all got put into groups so, we’re all a bit – it’s a industrial based project, and then each company – students were assigned to a company and then the company then gives you a problem to solve. So we’re all put in, we’re all split up and we’re all placed with a company and we’re given – that group of people, assigned to that company – certain people have been assigned as leaders for different groups, all working for the same company. And then we had to sign up our names against one of those leaders and one of the guys I worked with last year – that was my bad experience, I didn’t want to work with him again, the other lad my friend worked with last year. She said he was really good, so I was like I want to go with him. So I signed my name up (lost words)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And the team leaders that were selected, were they generally men?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I would say so, I think. I didn’t actually think of that at the time but yes. The trouble is that (?) if you’re the team leader you’re looking for some sort of erm knowledge about previous technical – like you might have worked on cars, you might know a bit about what’s going on in areas, all that kind of stuff. Girls don’t tend to – well I certainly – I still don’t – I’m learning now, but it’s only because I’m interested now, but I’ve no – they’ve got so much more confidence than us. I found that they were much more willing to go along and say that they knew something, even if they didn’t. It’d be like, you know, how do we do this? They’d say, oh I know how to do that and then come out with something and you’d think you know, and say, well I actually don’t know how to do this. I’m quite happy with someone else showing me how to do it. And they’re very confident in any ideas that they have, that they’re absolutely right and it’s always gonna work – and it’s not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s just men in general or do you think that the women aren’t as confident because they are in a male environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Personally, I would say I was about as confident of my ideas as they were but I couldn’t justify my confidence. I didn’t have the background knowledge to turn around and say to someone, this idea is definitely going to work because this equation shows this, this equation shows that. That was used in this previous product. I mean, I think girls are very much – they don’t make rash statements. They want to know that it’s right and it’s correct and you know, you can imagine (?) yourself when you come out of something, oh I’m right – I don’t have that problem.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what was the bad experience of working in the group then? …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: (I’d rather not say?). At the time it was working design project – for [company] – and we were put randomly into groups, a group of 5, me and my friend, both girls along with 3 of the lads. And we sat back on the design because we weren’t very confident and we didn’t really have any ideas, as a matter of fact (laughter) – it wasn’t what we were good at (yeah). It’s not that we’re girls and so we’re not good at it, it’s just that we’re not (?) – we prefer a different side of engineering to design. So when it came to an idea to move the sugar cube a certain distance along here, we had – we were coming up with ideas left, right and centre and we thought oh great, well this is nice that someone knows what they’re doing as well. But of course, they didn’t know what they were doing – they (lost words). So that went down first and then we got to the point where we had to virtually draw up our designs so we both went away and we said right, well cos’ you’ve done all the ideas, but we want to be part of the project as well, so we’ll go away and we’ll do these things on CAD so they gave us all the dimensions and we spent the whole weekend sitting on our – doing these autocad drawings and then when we met up the next week, they’d only gone away and changed the design and done the autocad drawings themselves and it was like, what? We’re all part of the designs really – because they had all the ideas and these 3 lads were friends, they used to go round each others houses a lot and they used to discuss things, like you do, and they’d come up with all these ideas and then make changes without consulting the rest of the group, which – I mean I’ve spoken to my dad about this and he was like – in this respect and he said, well they were only doing the project, which is true, they were but we weren’t included in that project.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you think that’s because they were mates and knew each other? Do you think if there were 2 lads in the group and they were friends it would’ve been the same, or it would’ve been the women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know – I couldn’t say but I know that our ideas weren’t listened to when we did have ideas. That was one part, one part was moving the sugar cube about the circuit, the other part was (?) the sugar cube down. And [name] and I, she’s the other girl – came up with an idea. Oh great. Like a (lost words) candy sweets, and thought that’s a good idea. So we went out to a shop, found a (??) in a pound shop, brought it in and showed the lads it. Right, that would work a treat. I said right, let’s get on with this. And they said, yeah, yeah, we’ll just wait till – one lad wasn’t with us at the time – we’ll just wait till he comes back and then we can work on it. And we were working quick and I said we aren’t very happy – we’ve contributed to the project, a found an idea – it’s not a complete idea but what a good idea it is. It’s very simple and we could adapt that, sort of thing. Next week he’s gone away, he’s changed the design, he’s drawn it up and he comes in with his thing and that’s what we’re stuck with, ‘cos that’s his idea and that’s what he wants to do. It was a good idea, so we’re stuck with it – but whoa, you know we’re over here and we did something towards that but they just totally blanked us and took it as their own and didn’t include us in any of the design. Aah, they did my head in. The worst part – the reason – the fact that we ended up – we ended up in tears at the end of the project, we were so upset with how things had gone already, and the CAD drawings and we’d done so much work on it, and they’d just come up with something else and then the day before it had to be handed in we all got together to try and get this thing working. It had a lot of electrics in it – not electronic engineers, we didn’t really know what we were doing but (???) we tried to follow it and it wasn’t going too well and eventually we got something working but then one of the lads said, I want to go home. I really don’t want to stay here anymore. I can’t be bothered. We can do this tomorrow morning. And then [name] decided to get out. He put – he probably didn’t realise it was going to happen – he lifted the whole thing up and like everything fell apart and [name] and I were in the process of labelling the wires, so that we knew where to put them together the next time, but he just ripped it all – ruined all we’d done. We said well you can go home now as long as we come back early the next day because we had to show this guy – our lecturer – show him our model, the working model. We don’t (lost words) make our model work at 10 O’clock. So we had to meet early (??) so we can get everything working, and then we can be able to show it. They said, yeh yeh yeh we’re going home. We were like alright then, fine ok. Next day 9 O’clock they’re not there. Where are they? They’re not here, oh dear, now it’s got to 10 O’clock – they’re still not here and we have to show this whole thing at 10. So we said OK, we’ll go down to the lab, [name] and I, we were the only ones there and they still weren’t here. 10 past 10 – Oh look, you’ve finally turned up have you? Is it working? No, but we’ve managed to spray paint it and it looks very pretty. I’m like what the hell? So everyone else was showing off theirs, and we was fiddling with it and trying to get it right and eventually we were the last group and we had to show it and it wasn’t working, and [name] and I both went into tears, we were so frustrated we couldn’t do anything about it. They had the model, they had the (?). They did all the designs themselves, they went away and did the project by themselves, without including us and it didn’t matter how much we tried, how much we wanted to input into it, and offered our services and our help, they just didn’t care. They didn’t care enough, and they were always quite happy getting a C on their project, whereas [name] and I wanted an A - and that’s something about girls, you’ll find, that they’re much more likely to be high achievers because they want that. They want the A’s whereas the lads, oh it’s first year I don’t care – quite happy with a C, maybe even a D. Who would you (??) right. They think they’re right.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, do you think that they don’t realise that team work isn’t just about the final outcome but actually learning skills by working in a team?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I think they were more – they wanted results, they wanted to win their competition. They wanted theirs to be better to someone else’s. They were always comparing it with some other group. So we ended up crying in the department, going in the girls loos and one of the secretary’s spotted us, dragged us out. She was like, right, what’s going on? So we told her and she said right, I’m not having this in my department. What’s going on. Our lecturer gets dragged in and he’s very angry and he pulled the lads and in the end, and had a word with them and said, you know, don’t carry on like this in this department. They were just being lads – they were being immature lads about it. They were being – they were making their little groups, making their little pack and doing their own thing and that’s what lads do. And that’s something I’ve had to deal with and make sure it doesn’t happen again. But one of the lads, that was in that group, he was the worst lad out of all of them and he – pretty much the other 2 sorted – there’s always one, I think if he’s re-taking, I’m happy (laughter). I’m in the 2nd year, he’s back in the 1st year now because he did absolutely no work. I don’t think much about him at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, so overall, the degree and the course, has it been what you’ve expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d say you don’t – I don’t think you can ever expect having to do this large amount of work. Whatever, I think doing engineering you sort of – you come out of A levels, you think God, that was much harder than GCSE’s, whereas God, A levels – hardest thing in the world. How can anything ever get harder than A levels? Then you go to degree level and you’re like aaargh, my goodness. How many subjects do I have to do? And how many tutorials and how many (??) and working in a group for the first time as well. Whenever I’ve worked in groups before – on school things, girls tend to stick together if you work in a group – well, it’s a load of girls, easy as that. You go do this, you go do that, I’d like to do this, is that OK? Yeah, Ok, fine, project done and thank you, A grade and there it is. Everyone wants to achieve high, and everyone wants to work together, and everyone can communicate fine and vice versa with the lads, the lads in my physics class worked together and they did it fine, and more often than not they’d get higher marks because they were brainy and intelligent, and we used to chat a lot (laugher). So it’s just – but I don’t think – I think both sexes aren’t used to working together. It must be worse for someone who’s come from an all boys school or an all girls school.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes its interesting speaking to those people.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: But I don’t, I’ve been to a mixed school all my life, and being (?) doesn’t really matter does it. But then girls always stay with girls and boys always stay with boys.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The course? The best things about the course – I really enjoy it and I get to do a large variety of subjects and I have some very, very intelligent lecturers, and amazing teachers amongst them. And I’ve met some amazing people through it, through coming to university and doing this degree and while I’ve been here I’ve met some amazing people, doing group work and all I think about these things and they come up with these ideas. (lost words)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, my next question’s probably related to that. Who or what do you think has been the biggest influence on you since you started this degree?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d say the lecturers and er one lecturer – you always get one don’t you wherever – in my foundation year I had a lecturer called (name) and he was a hero actually. He was (??) actually and er this year well (??) the year before that – right, the first year was last year and I’ve had the same lecturer this year and he’s been to (?) university and he’s amazing too. But he’s a really good teacher and if you need to go and talk to him, he’s there for you.. I mean he’s had a chat to me, several times, you see and he says do you know what you’re doing here? ‘cos I’ll go to him, moaning about something and he’ll say, oh have you thought about it this way before and I’m like no, actually, I haven’t. (laughter) And I just need someone to just (lost words) and stop me focussing on myself and just sort of see the bigger picture, and know that it’s not all about you. The other students all seem to be having the same problem. And a lot of time when you blame someone else, it’s usually your own fault – not fault, but something you could have done yourself and I mean, that – going back to that first year project, I mean I blame the lads did a lot of that, but my fault as well. I was in that project, I was a part of that group. I could have done something perhaps or attempted to communicate a bit more, made it known to our lecturer beforehand that I wasn’t – that this was the situation, because it had been going on for some time and just try to talk and communicate more and try and become more involved in the design phase, and, at the time, I thought I was doing enough but the end result wasn’t likeable and maybe there was something else I could have done. I can’t say what,, no point really thinking about it, you can’t go back.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you say that’s been the worst thing about the course? Is there anything else?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think – I think finding coming in to reality has been the worst thing on my course. Finding out that things aren’t as easy as you think they are and you might say to yourself, well if I’d have done that then I might have got those marks, but then when you go to try to do it, it’s really quite hard and that’s why no-one usually does do it, you know, it takes a lot of time and effort. It – the people I think – the lads that I was working with, in the first year, were fairly nice lads. When I spoke to them out of uni or whatever, it was nice chat and I wouldn’t have thought anything bad about them. turns.text: How do you think that you will deal with it if anything like that happens to you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: If I felt I was being neglected perhaps or not given the kind of work that I’d like, that’s something I’d make sure of when I started work – I’d make sure that they have got the systems in place to deal with things like that. A lot of companies do take it seriously now. It would take a lot of strength for a woman to go away and say I want this investigated. But I think – I think to be a woman in engineering nowadays, you have to have a lot of character, and you have to have a lot of confidence in yourself and that you were right and that you could have those problems sorted out. And if you do have that – you have to be confident purely to inspire confidence and until you show that you’re not as confident as them, they’ll take advantage of you and they’ll just be…you’ve just got to be as big and loud as you can be. In fact, or the other way be quiet and demure and come in with a quip, every now and then and maybe then they’ll be like, ah she’s quite (one?) to watch out for. Y’know, one of them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, the last thing that I’ve got to ask you is do you think that as an engineering student your educational experience differs from other students (yes) who are studying Social Science or Geography?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes (laughter) Big time, loads of hours, I have like a silly amount of hours, I think I’m up to 30 hours one week and it’s like madness.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that a good thing or a bad thing that you have more hours?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It pushes you. It pushes you so much and that’s fine because (Lost words)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it makes it easier when you actually go into work, if you have had as much structured time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ve heard from people that are graduating right now, that at university, especially with engineering is too technical, we have to cram so much into such a short bit of time but er you’re (?) and you’re working really hard and everyone in a company is really impressed with you because you can do the work as quickly. It’s only because they’ve got lazy and they don’t feel like doing it anymore and they slow down but you’re still working at this pace, that you do at university and eventually you calm it down and work at their pace ‘cos its easier and its accepted, so why not? I’ve heard that from a couple of people.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Well thank you very much.
